events.text: One night you look down at {pw_world} and do not see people. You see a field: the slow gold of their qi rising from every hearth and every temple, more of it than any pill or vein could ever give. A voice that sounds like your own says it plainly. It is yours. You made it. Nobody would ever have to know.

choices.text: Listen, and remember the way it was said

effects.log: You do not answer the voice. You do not forget it either. {pw_world} glows a little brighter in your sight from then on.
You turn away. The thought follows you to the door, and waits there, patient as a debt.

events.text: In the old books of the Upper Realm there is a page every immortal pretends not to have read. It tells of gods who raised a world the way a farmer raises rice: tended it, thinned it, and when it was heavy and gold, cut it all down at once. The page is about {pw_world}. It does not say so. It does not need to.

choices.text: Read the page to the end

effects.log: The page ends with a list of names. None of those gods are remembered by their worlds. All of them climbed very high.
The page burns badly, and leaves a smell on your fingers for a season.

events.text: You lean on the fate of {pw_world} the way a thumb leans on a scale, and in a village of {pw_people} a child is born who talks at four months and walks into the river at two to watch the qi move in it. The midwife calls it a blessing. The priests write it down. You write it down too, in a different book.

effects.log: You watch. The child grows quickly and well, and every year a little more qi rises from them into the sky.

choices.text: Give the child one good year first

effects.log: You send the child a year with no illness, no hunger and a best friend. It changes nothing you have planned. It is still a good year.

events.text: The genius you made is a quiet one: a young scholar of {pw_kingdom} who sits by the same well every evening and understands, one evening at a time, how the world was put together. One evening they look straight up at the sky and frown, as if something up there had been very slightly out of place.

effects.log: You close the sky. The scholar shakes their head, laughs at themself, and goes back to the well.
The scholar looks for a long time and writes one line in their notebook: "the stars are counting us." Then they go home.

events.text: A fighter is born in {pw_world} who wins every bout of the village fair before they are twelve, and laughs every time, and is loved for the laugh more than for the winning. The elders of {pw_kingdom} send for them. Their qi is a bright thread already, and it pulls up into the dark above the world like smoke from a lamp.

effects.log: You pull, gently. The fighter trains harder that year than anyone in the world has ever trained, and never knows why.
The fighter keeps the laugh. It is the one thing in this you leave untouched.

events.text: A healer of {pw_people}, nine years old, puts their hands on a dying grandmother and the grandmother gets up and makes soup. By the end of the year there is a queue at their door a mile long. Every person they heal goes home carrying a little of the healer's qi, and every night that qi drifts upward to you.

effects.log: The queue grows. The healer grows thin. The sky over {pw_world} grows bright.

choices.text: Send the healer a night of rest

effects.log: One night the queue goes home early for no reason. The healer sleeps until noon, the only long sleep of their life.

events.text: In {pw_world} there is a child who sees the old roads: they walk out at dawn and come back at dusk with stories of paths no map shows, and every road they find carries qi to the great cities a little faster. The people of {pw_kingdom} call them the Road-Finder. You call them the fifth sheaf.

choices.text: Point them at the richest road

effects.log: The Road-Finder finds the richest road in the world and follows it for the rest of their life.
The Road-Finder finds a road to a valley of white flowers, and builds a house there, and is happy for a while.

events.text: It takes very little. A fire at a border shrine, a dream sent to two proud elders on the same night, a rumour carried on the wind of {pw_world} a little further than it should go. By spring two peoples who traded salt for a thousand years are burning each other's fields, and every soldier who falls gives up their qi to the sky.

effects.log: The qi of the dead rises like heat off a summer road. You gather it in. It tastes of iron and of salt.

choices.text: Keep the war away from the children

effects.log: You keep the war on the roads and the fields, away from the villages. It is a strange mercy, and it costs you a little qi.

events.text: The priests of both sides pray to you on the same morning, in the same words: give us victory. You listen to both, and answer neither, and the war in {pw_world} goes on another generation. A general of {pw_kingdom} kneels in an empty temple at night and asks only why. Nobody tells them.

effects.log: The general waits until dawn, then gets up and goes back to the war.

choices.text: Send the general a dream of home

effects.log: The general dreams of their mother's kitchen. In the morning they sign a truce for the winter, and the war takes its rest.

events.text: In {pw_world} two kings receive the same omen, a comet over the same mountain, and each is told by their astrologers that the mountain is theirs by heaven's will. They are both right, in a way. You sent the comet. By the end of the century one kingdom is gone, and the field of its last battle glows to your eyes for a hundred years.

effects.log: You drink. The field goes grey. The farmers who come back to it later say nothing will grow there for a while.

choices.text: Leave the field to the farmers

effects.log: You leave the field. Barley grows there within ten years, unusually tall.

events.text: A young soldier of {pw_people} drops their spear in the middle of a battle and starts to sing, an old song of the first people of {pw_world}, and for a moment the soldiers on both sides lower their weapons and listen. It is a small moment. It would be very easy to end it.

effects.log: Somebody on the far side throws first. The song stops, and the battle goes on, and the qi rises.
The song finishes. The battle goes on afterwards, but for the rest of that war, nobody fights on that hill again.

events.text: An old priest of {pw_world}, blind for twenty years, reads the omens backwards one winter and understands: the prodigies, the wars, the comet, all of it. "The god is fattening us," the priest tells the high temple, very calmly. Nobody believes it at first. Then somebody counts the geniuses born in the last hundred years.

choices.text: Let them believe what they like

effects.log: The temples of {pw_world} go quiet, and then they go to another god: one who promises to protect them from the sky.

choices.text: Send the priest a vision to unsay it

effects.log: The vision is a lie, and the old priest knows it, and says so, and dies a year later still saying so. It costs you to lie that loudly.

events.text: In the market squares of {pw_kingdom} a new song is going round, one the children sing while skipping. It is about a farmer in the sky who grows people like rice. The temple guards try to stop it. You cannot stop a skipping song. The faith of {pw_world} drains away like water out of a cracked bowl.

effects.log: It is a good song. The rhymes are clever. You find yourself humming it, and stop.

choices.text: Send a blessing to buy them back

effects.log: The harvest is good that year. The children sing the song anyway, a little more quietly.

events.text: You open your mouth over {pw_world} and drink. The rivers dim first, then the fields, then the cities; the qi of every genius you raised comes up in one bright rope. The gods of {pw_heaven} try to hold the sky shut and are torn out of it like paper. When it is over, you are fuller than you have ever been, and below you a few thousand people walk out of the dust and look up.

effects.log: You look down. They are looking up. Neither of you looks away for a long time.
You do not look back. The weight of the world's qi settles in your dantian like a stone in a river, and it is very easy, after all.

events.text: The second time is easier, which is the worst thing about it. {pw_world} had rebuilt so well: new kingdoms, new temples, new children who thought the old story of the sky that drinks was a story. You drink it again, and the gold goes out of it again, and the qi fills you like a tide that knows the way.

effects.log: You count it. It is more than last time. The world grew richer for having been ruined once.

choices.text: Remember one face from the last harvest

effects.log: You remember a face from last time, and it hurts, and the hurt is the only thing in you that is not full.

events.text: In {pw_world} the survivors of the last harvest built their temples low and their houses deep, and told their grandchildren to watch the sky. Their grandchildren forgot. You come back for the harvest in the year {pw_years} of the world, and only a few old people in the hills see it coming, and run.

choices.text: Let the old people in the hills go

effects.log: You leave the hills alone. Whatever the world becomes next, it will be built by people who remember.
You take the hills too. The next generation of {pw_world} will have no one to warn it.

events.text: Four centuries after the harvest, villages stand again along the old rivers of {pw_world}. The people build with the stones of the old temples, and do not build new ones; they bury their dead facing away from the sky. In a school in a rebuilt town, a teacher draws the world on a slate, and leaves the sky off the drawing.

effects.log: You watch the school for a whole year. Nobody in it mentions you once.

choices.text: Send the teacher one warm spring

effects.log: The spring is warm and long. The teacher takes the children out to see the fields, and for once nobody looks up.

events.text: The survivors of {pw_world} have a word now that their grandparents did not need: it means the year the sky opened. They say it the way other worlds say plague, or flood. A child asks why the gods let it happen. The old woman telling the story says the gods did not let it. The gods were the first to go.

choices.text: Listen to the rest of the story

effects.log: The story ends badly for the sky. It is not true, not yet. You find you want to hear it again.

choices.text: Leave a little rain on the fields

effects.log: The rain comes at the right time for the first time in a long time. The old woman says it means nothing. She plants anyway.

events.text: {pw_world} is whole again. Its fields are gold, its rivers bright, its people many; new kingdoms argue over old borders, and new temples have gone up to gods who are not you, or who are you under other names. The qi rises from every hearth as it did before. Nobody below believes the old story about the sky. It would be very easy.

effects.log: You look at the field, and the field is ripe, and you have done this before.

choices.text: Let it be a world this time

effects.log: You let it be a world this time. It is harder than the harvest was.

events.text: In the rebuilt {pw_world} a child finds a grey stone in a field where nothing used to grow, and takes it to a priest, and the priest, who is very old, goes pale. It is a piece of the old high temple, from before the year the sky opened. The priest gives it back to the child and says: keep it, and keep looking up.

effects.log: The child keeps the stone all their life. Their grandchildren keep it after them, on a shelf, facing the window.
In a few winters the stone is a pebble like any other. The child forgets where they put it.

events.text: You grow up in {pw_world} among stones that used to be a city. The old people say there were kingdoms here once, and gods in the sky, and a temple so tall its bell could be heard across three rivers. Then the sky opened. Everyone you know is descended from the few who walked out of the dust.

choices.text: Ask the oldest person what they remember

effects.log: They remember a light going out of everything at once, like a lamp. They do not remember anything after that for a week.
You clear stones all summer. In autumn there is a field where there was not, and the old people come to look at it.

events.text: In the ruins of {pw_world} there is a broken shrine to a god who fell from {pw_heaven} on the day the sky opened. Nobody prays there. Nobody pulls it down either. You find it one evening, overgrown, with a cracked face that looks, if you tilt your head, as if it is crying.

effects.log: You clean it. By spring there are wild flowers in front of it every morning, and you are not the one leaving them.
You leave it. Some things should be allowed to finish falling.

events.text: The people of {pw_world} bury their dead facing away from the sky, and teach their children never to pray out loud. You ask your neighbour why, once, when you are small. Your neighbour puts down the spade and says: because it listens. Then they pick the spade up again and do not say anything more about it for the rest of their life.

effects.log: You whisper a prayer at the top of the hill. Nothing answers. You feel, very strongly, that something heard.

choices.text: Keep the silence like everyone else

effects.log: You keep it. It is a hard world, but it is a quiet one.

events.text: A trader comes through the village with a cart of things dug out of the old cities of {pw_world}: a bronze bell, a jade seal, a child's shoe. They say the cities stood for a thousand years. They say everything in them died in one afternoon, the rats and the birds too. They say it as if it were weather.

choices.text: Buy the child's shoe and bury it

effects.log: You bury it under the oldest tree in the village. You do not tell anyone why.

choices.text: Ask the trader what did it

effects.log: The trader looks up at the sky for a long moment, then changes the subject to the price of salt.

events.text: In {pw_world} the children have a game called The Sky That Drinks: one child is the sky, and everyone else runs, and whoever the sky touches has to lie down and be very still. The grown-ups do not like the game, and cannot say why. An old woman of the village stops you playing it once, quite sharply, and then apologises.

choices.text: Ask the old woman about it

effects.log: She says it is an old story, and that old stories are not always only stories. Then she makes you tea.
You teach the others a game about building a city instead. It catches on, slowly.

events.text: The new temples of {pw_world} are built low, with no towers, and their priests teach that the old god died in the year the sky opened, and that this is good news. You sit at the back of one of their sermons and are surprised to find yourself angry, as if somebody were telling a lie about you.

effects.log: You stay. The priest is kind, and the sermon is wise, and you leave feeling you owe somebody an apology.
You leave. On the steps outside you find you are looking up, and make yourself stop.

events.text: There is a prodigy in your part of {pw_world}, the kind of genius who comes once a century, and you know them: you grew up two doors apart. Lately they have grown thin and bright-eyed and cannot stop training, and one night they tell you they dream of the sky every night, and in the dream the sky is hungry.

choices.text: Tell them to hide their gift

effects.log: They laugh, and then they do not laugh, and the next year they put down their sword and become a carpenter. The dreams stop.

choices.text: Tell them it is only a dream

effects.log: They thank you, and go back to training, and the dreams go on.

events.text: In {pw_world} the prodigies are being born closer and closer together: the priests are delighted and the old farmers are frightened, and you are the only one who notices that the farmers are right. It is the way a field looks, the old ones say, in the last weeks before the cutting.

choices.text: Go to the priests with it

effects.log: The priests laugh at you, mostly. One of them follows you out and asks you to say it again, slowly.
The farmers nod and say nothing, and start storing seed in deep places.

events.text: The war came to {pw_world} out of nowhere: a burned shrine, a bad dream, and now two peoples who traded salt for a thousand years are killing each other on the roads. A deserter from the other side hides in your barn. They tell you nobody on their side knows why the war started either, and that the dead look peaceful, as if something drank the pain out of them.

choices.text: Hide them until it is safe

effects.log: You hide them through the winter. In spring they walk home along the river, and write to you every year after.

choices.text: Ask them more about the dead

effects.log: You ask, and they tell you, and you go to the temple with it. The priests write it down, uneasily.

events.text: An old priest of {pw_world} is preaching in the square, and the guards are trying to move them on. The priest is saying that the god who made the world is not good: that it raises geniuses the way a farmer raises pigs, and starts wars for the qi of the dead. Most people laugh. You do not.

choices.text: Help the priest get away from the guards

effects.log: You hide the priest for three nights. They go on preaching in other towns, and some of what they say begins to stick.
You walk on. The priest's voice follows you all the way down the street.

events.text: In a library of {pw_world} you find a book nobody has opened in a long time: a history of the year the sky opened, written by someone who saw it. The last page says the sky has done it before, in some other world, and will do it again here when the fields are full, and that the only defence is to remember. You feel strange holding it, as if it were a letter addressed to you.

choices.text: Copy it out and give it away

effects.log: You copy it out ten times and leave the copies in ten temples. By the end of your life there are hundreds.

choices.text: Put it back on the shelf

effects.log: You put it back. On the way out you look up at the sky, and the sky, you are fairly sure, looks back.
